fuentes/codigo-de-lipit-ishtar/resumen.texto: Collection of laws in Sumerian attributed to Lipit-Ishtar of Isin, a century older than the code of Hammurabi. It was copied in scribal education for centuries after his death.

fuentes/codigo-de-lipit-ishtar/por_que_i.texto: It is one of the direct antecedents of the legal tradition that culminates in the code of Hammurabi.

fuentes/leyes-de-eshnunna/resumen.texto: Collection of laws inscribed on two tablets found at Tell Harmal (Shaduppum) in 1945 and 1947, copies of an older source from c. 1930 BC. A later fragment appeared at Me-Turan.

fuentes/leyes-de-eshnunna/por_que_import.texto: The differences from the code of Hammurabi help trace the development of cuneiform law; unlike other Mesopotamian collections, it is not presented as the work of a king.

fuentes/atrahasis/resumen.texto: Akkadian epic known in several versions, which tells of the creation of humanity to serve the gods, its multiplication and a flood. The oldest known copy is dated by its colophon to the reign of Ammi-saduqa (1646-1626 BC), and there are also Old Babylonian fragments.

fuentes/atrahasis/por_que_importa.texto: It is the antecedent of the flood account in the Epic of Gilgamesh.

fuentes/enuma-elis/resumen.texto: Babylonian myth of creation that narrates a battle of the gods, the rise of Marduk, the creation of humanity, and ends with praise of Marduk. The oldest known manuscript is from the 9th century BC, found at Assur.

fuentes/enuma-elis/por_que_importa.texto: Its date is disputed: it was once believed to have been composed in the time of Hammurabi, but most specialists today place it in the Second Dynasty of Isin, at the end of the second millennium.

fuentes/tablilla-de-venus-de-ammisaduqa/.texto: Record of the positions of Venus, tablet 63 of the Enuma Anu Enlil, preserved in copies from the first millennium BC. The original record is thought to have been compiled in the time of Ammi-saduqa.
It is used to date the first dynasty of Babylon: readings of it have produced the long, middle, short and ultra-short chronologies.

fuentes/plimpton-322/resumen.texto: Broken Old Babylonian clay tablet with a mathematical table in cuneiform writing whose rows relate to Pythagorean triples. It is dated to c. 1800 BC on the basis of the script style, typical of southern Iraq; the merchant who sold it said it came from Senkereh (Larsa) and, judging by its format, it could be from Larsa, c. 1822-1784 BC.

fuentes/plimpton-322/por_que_importa.texto: Its interpretation is debated; Robson argues that the author was probably a scribe working with exercises from scribal education.

fuentes/ybc-7289/resumen.texto: Babylonian tablet with a precise sexagesimal approximation of the square root of 2, the diagonal of a unit square. It is attributed to a student from southern Mesopotamia between 1800 and 1600 BC.

fuentes/ybc-7289/por_que_importa.texto: It shows the level of computational precision reached in antiquity, equivalent to six decimal places.

fuentes/matematica-paleobabilonica/resum.texto: Set of school tablets with tables, problems and calculations in the sexagesimal system, among them Plimpton 322 and YBC 7289. They include calculations of areas and roots.

fuentes/matematica-paleobabilonica/por_q.texto: They document the mathematics of the scribal schools of the time of Hammurabi and his successors.

fuentes/archivos-de-mari/resumen.texto: Several thousand tablets found since 1933 in the palace of Mari, at Tell Hariri, almost all from the early 18th century BC, before the destruction of the city. At least 9000 have been published, out of an estimated 19 000 tablets and fragments.

fuentes/archivos-de-mari/por_que_importa.texto: They are the main source for international relations in the 18th century BC; for the 14th century BC, the Amarna Letters play a similar role.

fuentes/archivos-de-kanesh/resumen.texto: More than 23 000 cuneiform tablets found in the lower city of Kültepe (ancient Kanesh), where the karum, the commercial quarter of the Assyrian merchants, existed. They are the main archive of Old Assyrian trade.

fuentes/archivos-de-kanesh/por_que_impor.texto: They document the activity of the merchants of Assur in Anatolia and the dating by Assyrian eponyms (limmu).

fuentes/archivos-de-kanesh/leer.0.titulo.texto: Catalogue of the Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative, with Kanesh tablets

fuentes/lista-real-asiria/resumen.texto: List of Assyrian kings based on the annual eponyms (limmu), in copies from Assur, Dur-Sharrukin and Nineveh. The regnal years are generally accepted, but part of the list is fictitious and some known kings are missing from it.

fuentes/lista-real-asiria/por_que_import.texto: The date of its composition is disputed: it was once attributed to Shamshi-Adad I, and today it is placed much later, perhaps in the time of Ashurnasirpal I.

fuentes/lista-real-babilonica/resumen.texto: Set of lists of kings of Babylon: List A (BM 33332) runs from Sumu-abum to Kandalanu, List B records the first dynasty and the first dynasty of the Sealand, and List C preserves part of the second dynasty of Isin.

fuentes/lista-real-babilonica/por_que_im.texto: They are the basis for reconstructing the succession of kings and dynasties of Babylon, although the early parts of the Kassite dynasty are damaged.

fuentes/ludlul-bel-nemeqi/resumen.texto: Akkadian poem, called “of the righteous sufferer”, about the unjust suffering of a righteous man, which may be a hymn of thanksgiving to Marduk for his healing. Its composition is dated to the reign of the Kassite king Nazi-Maruttash, named in line 105 of tablet IV.

fuentes/ludlul-bel-nemeqi/por_que_import.texto: It is an example of Kassite wisdom literature on the problem of evil.

fuentes/enuma-anu-enlil/resumen.texto: Great series of astral omens with between 6500 and 7000 omens about celestial and atmospheric phenomena, concerning the king and the state. It includes the Venus tablet of Ammi-saduqa.

fuentes/enuma-anu-enlil/por_que_importa.texto: It is the major work of Babylonian astrology; its earliest forms are linked to the second millennium.

fuentes/leyes-asirias-medias/resumen.texto: Three law collections found at Assur and developed between 1450 and 1250 BC in the Middle Assyrian Empire. The first copy to be discovered dates from the reign of Tiglath-pileser I.

fuentes/leyes-asirias-medias/por_que_imp.texto: They are similar to Sumerian and Babylonian law but with generally harsher penalties, such as the mutilation of ears and noses.

fuentes/kudurrus-casitas/resumen.texto: Boundary stones recording land grants to vassals by the Kassite kings and their successors. The original was kept in the temple and the beneficiary received a clay copy.

fuentes/kudurrus-casitas/por_que_importa.texto: They document property, privileges and kings with their dates; they are the basis for Kassite history.

fuentes/ancient-iraq-roux/resumen.texto: General history of Mesopotamia by the French writer Georges Roux, published in English in 1964 (reissued in 1972 and 1992) by Penguin Books.

fuentes/ancient-iraq-roux/por_que_import.texto: It covers the history of Mesopotamia from its origins, including Isin and Larsa, the Babylon of Hammurabi, the Kassites and Assyria.

fuentes/van-de-mieroop-near-east/titulo.texto: A History of the Ancient Near East ca. 3000-323 BC

fuentes/van-de-mieroop-near-east/resumen.texto: History of the ancient Near East by the historian Marc Van De Mieroop, Wiley-Blackwell edition of 2015. It covers Isin and Larsa, Hammurabi, Shamshi-Adad I and Mari.

fuentes/van-de-mieroop-near-east/por_que.texto: It is an academic synthesis of the history of the ancient Near East, dealing with the Amorite dynasties, Hammurabi, Shamshi-Adad I and Mari.

fuentes/im-67118/resumen.texto: Old Babylonian tablet in the Iraq Museum that solves a problem of plane geometry about a rectangle of given area and diagonal; in its last part it checks the solution with the Pythagorean theorem. It was excavated in 1962 at Tell al-Dhiba'i, which depended on the kingdom of Eshnunna, and is dated to c. 1770 BC (middle chronology), in the time of Ibal-pi-El II.

fuentes/im-67118/por_que_importa.texto: The steps of the solution are interpreted as operations of cutting and pasting figures on a diagram, from which it has been suggested that the Mesopotamians may have derived the Pythagorean theorem earlier.

fuentes/dialogo-entre-un-hombre-y-su-dio.texto: Dialogue between a Man and His God

Wisdom text preserved on a single tablet, attributed in its last line to a certain Kalbanum, about whom nothing else is known. It is the oldest known text that treats the question of why a god allows evil. Lambert dates it to the reign of Ammi-ditana, in the late phase of the Old Babylonian period.
It anticipates in Akkadian the theme of the suffering of the righteous that reappears in Ludlul bel nemeqi and in the Babylonian Theodicy.

fuentes/teodicea-babilonica/resumen.texto: Akkadian poem in the form of a dialogue between a sufferer and his friend about human suffering and the possibility of a moral order in the world. It is composed as an acrostic in 27 stanzas of 11 lines each, whose message names Saggil-kinam-ubbib, a priest-exorcist. The oldest manuscripts are from the reign of Ashurbanipal; from the language it is placed after the Kassite period, around 1000 BC.

fuentes/teodicea-babilonica/por_que_impo.texto: It is compared with the Book of Job. Its date ranges between 1600 and 900 BC according to different authors, so it closes the series of second-millennium wisdom texts without belonging to it with certainty.

fuentes/consejos-de-sabiduria/resumen.texto: Akkadian wisdom text of moral exhortations, made mostly of two-line units. The manuscripts are fragmentary and the original would have had about 160 lines; its composition is placed around the first dynasty of Babylon. Lambert published a translation of the preserved parts in 1996.

fuentes/consejos-de-sabiduria/por_que_im.texto: It shows the genre of moral counsel in Akkadian at the time of the first dynasty of Babylon.

fuentes/cronica-dinastica/resumen.texto: Fragmentary bilingual text, in six columns and preserved in at least four copies, which continues the tradition of the Sumerian King List down to the 8th century BC. It begins with nine antediluvian kings of five cities and an account of the flood, and goes on with the successive dynasties of Babylon. Thorkild Jacobsen considered it a variant of the King List.

fuentes/cronica-dinastica/por_que_import.texto: It is a source for reconstructing periods poorly preserved in other texts, such as the dynasties of the second millennium, although its copies are late.

fuentes/cronica-dinastica/leer.0.titulo.texto: Translation of the Dynastic Chronicle (ABC 18) on Livius

fuentes/lamento-por-nippur/escrita.lugar.texto: Mesopotamia (tablet in the Penn Museum, provenance not determined)

fuentes/lamento-por-nippur/resumen.texto: Sumerian lament, known by its opening “tur3 me nun-e”, one of the five “city laments” in which the patron goddess mourns the ruin of her city. It consists of nine songs with eight antiphons and three further songs; in the final part King Ishme-Dagan is presented restoring Nippur. It is preserved in the Penn Museum and dated to the Old Babylonian period.

fuentes/lamento-por-nippur/por_que_impor.texto: It belongs to the literature of laments composed in the time of Isin and Larsa, for which the destruction of cities was a central theme.

fuentes/lamento-por-uruk/resumen.texto: Sumerian lament on the ruin of Uruk in the voice of its goddess, recited by the gala chanters. It is inspired by the Lament for Ur; it is dated to the Isin-Larsa period, around 1940 BC, and was copied again in the Hellenistic period.

fuentes/lamento-por-uruk/por_que_importa.texto: It is an example of the spread of the city-lament genre after the fall of Ur III.

fuentes/urra-hubullu/resumen.texto: Babylonian glossary of Sumerian-Akkadian lexical lists ordered by topic, which in its canonical version runs to 24 tablets and almost 10 000 words. Its name is its first gloss: “ur5-ra” and “hubullu”, “debt with interest”. There is a bilingual Sumerian-Hurrian version from Ugarit.

fuentes/urra-hubullu/por_que_importa.texto: Much of the collection was compiled in the Old Babylonian period, with earlier antecedents, and there was a bilingual tradition in Kassite times.

fuentes/nabnitu/resumen.texto: Old Babylonian encyclopedic work (c. 1800 BC) in several tablets, whose name is the first word of the first tablet, “Creation”. One tablet gives the technical names of the parts of the hand, another deals with domestic animals, and others with human actions.

fuentes/nabnitu/por_que_importa.texto: It shows the work of arranging knowledge into lists in the Old Babylonian scribal schools.

fuentes/el-pobre-de-nippur/resumen.texto: Akkadian tale from c. 1500 BC, preserved in only three texts, one of them almost complete. It tells how Gimil-Ninurta, a poor citizen of Nippur whom the mayor humiliates, takes revenge on him three times with disguises and deceptions.

fuentes/el-pobre-de-nippur/por_que_impor.texto: It is a story with a protagonist of humble condition who takes revenge on an official, within Akkadian literature of the second millennium.

fuentes/carta-de-iddin-sin-a-zinu/resume.texto: Old Babylonian letter from a student, Iddin-Sin, to his mother Zinu, believed to have been written at Larsa in the 18th century BC, around the reign of Hammurabi. He complains about the clothes she wove for him, worse than those of his classmates, and that even the adopted son of a servant of his father dressed better.

fuentes/carta-de-iddin-sin-a-zinu/por_qu.texto: It is a frequently cited witness to the daily life of scribal students.

fuentes/tablilla-de-queja-a-ea-nasir/res.texto: Akkadian tablet of c. 1750 BC that a dissatisfied customer sent to Ea-nasir, a copper merchant of Ur. Leonard Woolley found it among other similar complaints, and it is in the British Museum.

fuentes/tablilla-de-queja-a-ea-nasir/por.texto: It documents the copper trade and the relations between merchants and customers in Ur around the mid-18th century BC.

fuentes/kudurru-de-nazi-maruttash/resume.texto: Boundary stone (kudurru) of the Kassite king Nazi-Maruttash, found at Susa and now in the Louvre. Instead of registers with figures of gods, it uses graphic symbols, and it invokes the curse of nineteen deities against anyone who damages it.

fuentes/kudurru-de-nazi-maruttash/por_qu.texto: It is an example of a royal kudurru of the 13th century BC, with the list of gods who guarantee the grant.

fuentes/kudurru-de-kashtiliash-iv/resume.texto: Fragment of a kudurru recording the legal action of Kashtiliash IV over lands previously granted by Kurigalzu II to Uzub-Shiha (or Uzub-Shipak) in recognition of his service in the war against Assyria under Enlil-nirari. Together with the tablet of Akaptaha, they are the only surviving kudurrus of that reign, and both were recovered at Susa, where the Elamites had taken them.

fuentes/kudurru-de-kashtiliash-iv/por_qu.texto: It confirms from a Kassite document a war between Babylon and Assyria in the time of Enlil-nirari.

fuentes/kudurru-de-gula/resumen.texto: Boundary stone of the goddess Gula, from Kassite Babylon of the 14th-13th centuries BC, preserved in the Louvre. It shows Gula seated on her throne with her dog; the other side has registers with symbols of gods and sections of cuneiform text.

fuentes/kudurru-de-gula/por_que_importa.texto: It illustrates the divine iconography of Kassite kudurrus.

fuentes/herencia-de-takil-ana-ilishu/tit.texto: Kudurru of the Inheritance of Takil-ana-ilishu

fuentes/herencia-de-takil-ana-ilishu/res.texto: Stele from the late Kassite period recording a lawsuit over a disputed inheritance across three generations, more than forty years. It describes the recovery of family property or a claim of lineage and gives much information on inheritance in the late Bronze Age. Its colophon declares it a copy of three documents sealed with royal edicts.

fuentes/herencia-de-takil-ana-ilishu/por.texto: It is a source of Kassite private law, distinct from the royal land grants.

fuentes/concesion-a-marduk-apla-iddina/r.texto: Kudurru in which the Kassite king Meli-Shipak II grants four cultivated plots with their villages, in total 84 gur and 160 qa, to his servant Marduk-apla-iddina, who may be his son and successor or another person of the same name. The size of the grant and the exemption from all territorial obligations (taxes, corvée, conscription, forage) are exceptional.

fuentes/concesion-a-marduk-apla-iddina/p.texto: It is one of the kudurrus that support the chronology of the last Kassite kings.

fuentes/concesion-a-hunnubat-nanaya/resu.texto: Kudurru by which the Kassite king Meli-Shipak II gives his daughter 40 gur (about a thousand acres) of uncultivated land and control of three villages, with exemptions for the villages of the area guaranteed by a sealed tablet. A French team under Jacques de Morgan excavated it at Susa at the beginning of the 20th century.

fuentes/concesion-a-hunnubat-nanaya/por_.texto: It is a royal grant of land to a king's daughter.

fuentes/estela-de-meli-shipak/resumen.texto: Lower part of a large stele with reliefs and remains of inscriptions in Akkadian and Elamite. Shutruk-Nahhunte I took it as booty in his invasion of Babylon, when he deposed Zababa-shuma-iddina, and it was found at Susa between 1900 and 1904 in a courtyard next to the main temple, where there seems to have been a museum of trophies and offerings to Inshushinak.

fuentes/estela-de-meli-shipak/por_que_im.texto: It is one of the pieces carried to Susa after the Elamite sack of Babylon.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-1/resumen.texto: Letter from the pharaoh Amenhotep III to the Kassite king Kadashman-Enlil I, the first of the series of fourteen Amarna letters between Egypt and Babylon (EA 1 to EA 14). Only EA 1 and EA 5 were sent from Egypt to Babylon; the other twelve were written by Babylonians.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-1/por_que_imp.texto: It opens the correspondence with Babylon and fixes a synchronism between Amenhotep III and Kadashman-Enlil I.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-2/resumen.texto: Letter from Kadashman-Enlil I to Amenhotep III, continuing EA 1. It deals with a marriage proposal.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-2/por_que_imp.texto: It shows the diplomacy of marriages between courts in the time of Amenhotep III.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-3/resumen.texto: Letter from Kadashman-Enlil I to Amenhotep III, which Moran titles “Marriage, complaints, opening of a palace”. It is part of the series of letters from Babylon to Egypt.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-3/por_que_imp.texto: It is part of the exchange of letters on marriages and gifts between the two courts.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-4/resumen.texto: Letter from Kadashman-Enlil I to Amenhotep III, which Moran titles “Royal deceit and threats”. It continues the correspondence with EA 1 to 3 and alludes to a request for marriage to one of the pharaoh's daughters.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-4/por_que_imp.texto: It shows the tone of complaints between kings who called each other “brothers”.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-5/resumen.texto: Letter from Amenhotep III to Kadashman-Enlil I. It is known from two tablets, one in the British Museum (BM 29787) and one in the Egyptian Museum (C 12195); it is the other letter of the series sent from Egypt to Babylon.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-5/por_que_imp.texto: Together with EA 1, it is one of the two letters of the Babylonian series sent from Egypt.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-6/resumen.texto: Letter from Burna-Buriash II to the pharaoh Amenhotep III, dealing with gifts between the two kings. It belongs to the series of Babylonian letters to Egypt (EA 2 to 4 and EA 6 to 14).

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-6/por_que_imp.texto: It shows the exchange of gifts between Babylon and Egypt.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-7/resumen.texto: Letter from Burna-Buriash II, king of Karaduniash, to Napkhururiya, the pharaoh Akhenaten, showing the trade routes across the Levant. The tablet was destroyed in a bombing.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-7/por_que_imp.texto: It documents the passage of Babylonian caravans through the Levant.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-8/resumen.texto: Letter from Burna-Buriash II to Napkhururiya (Akhenaten), continuing EA 7, dated between 1349 and 1334 BC. Moran edits it with Ebeling's translation.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-8/por_que_imp.texto: It completes the correspondence of Burna-Buriash II with Akhenaten.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-9/resumen.texto: Letter from Burna-Buriash II to the pharaoh, on a tall, compact tablet of 38 lines and three paragraphs, in an almost intact state. Babylon appears as the most distant country writing to Egypt.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-9/por_que_imp.texto: It is one of the best-preserved Babylonian letters in the archive.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-10/resumen.texto: Letter from Burna-Buriash II to Amenhotep IV (Akhenaten), continuing the earlier correspondence. Together with EA 11 it has been used to argue that the pharaoh married two of his daughters, Meritaten and Ankhesenpaaten.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-10/por_que_im.texto: Its content feeds discussions about Akhenaten's family.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-11/resumen.texto: Letter from Burna-Buriash II to Akhenaten, on a badly damaged tablet. Its content suggests there was an epidemic at Amarna, and together with EA 10 it has been used to argue that the pharaoh married two of his daughters when they were about eleven or twelve years old.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-11/por_que_im.texto: Together with EA 10, it provides evidence of an epidemic and of Akhenaten's family.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-12/resumen.texto: Letter from a princess of Babylon to the king of Egypt, which mentions a scribe named Kidin-Adad. Part of the tablet reached the Vorderasiatisches Museum in 1888 through a donation by J. Simon, and another part through one by Felix von Niemeyer.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-12/por_que_im.texto: It is counted among the letters from Babylon to Egypt (EA 2 to 4 and EA 6 to 14).

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-15/resumen.texto: Letter from Ashur-uballit I of Assyria to the pharaoh, titled “Assyria enters the international scene”. It speaks of the motive of the Assyrian messenger, who goes to Egypt “to see” the country, and of the lack of contact between the two kingdoms for a time.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-15/por_que_im.texto: It marks the entry of Assyria into international diplomatic correspondence.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-16/resumen.texto: Letter from Ashur-uballit I, founder of the Middle Assyrian Empire, to an uncertain pharaoh: most specialists read the broken name as the prenomen of Akhenaten, but it could be that of Ay.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-16/por_que_im.texto: It shows the foreign policy of Ashur-uballit I toward Egypt.

fuentes/van-de-mieroop-king-hammurabi/re.texto: Political biography of King Hammurabi of Babylon by the historian Marc Van De Mieroop, published by Blackwell in 2005, in Oxford.

fuentes/van-de-mieroop-king-hammurabi/po.texto: It narrates Hammurabi's rise and his wars against Larsa, Eshnunna, Mari and the northern kingdoms.

fuentes/inscripcion-de-agum-kakrime/resu.texto: Akkadian text written in Neo-Assyrian signs with very short lines, imitating an archaizing style, preserved in two copies from Nineveh (one from the library of Ashurbanipal); the origin of the original is unknown. It tells how Agum-kakrime recovered from the land of Hana the statue of Marduk that the Hittites had carried off in the sack of Babylon and restored it to the renewed Esagila, and it lists his donations to the temple.

fuentes/inscripcion-de-agum-kakrime/por_.texto: It is the source of the tradition about the return of Marduk's statue under Agum II. Its authenticity is disputed: some see it as late propaganda for the cult of Marduk and others defend it; everything known about Agum-kakrime comes from this text.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-dur-untash/resu.texto: Bricks from the ziggurat and sacred precinct of Chogha Zanbil with cuneiform inscriptions giving the names of gods in Elamite and Akkadian; one of them, found by a geologist, described the construction of a sacred city by “Untash-Gal”. Another mentions a gold statue dedicated to the god Nahhunte.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-dur-untash/por_.texto: They document the founding of Dur-Untash by Untash-Napirisha and his cult of Inshushinak.

fuentes/ladrillos-de-adad-nirari-i-en-ki.texto: Brick Molds of Adad-nirari I at Kilizu
Four brick molds found in 2018 at Qasr Shemamok, celebrating the construction of a palace at Kilizu by the Assyrian king Adad-nirari I.
They are direct evidence of Middle Assyrian building works at Kilizu.

fuentes/cronica-de-eponimos-de-mari/resu.texto: The oldest eponym chronicle, compiled at Mari in the 18th century BC and preserved in eleven fragments found in the royal palace. It records at least one notable event per year, together with the name of an official, for the years before and during the reign of Shamshi-Adad I; M. Birot first edited it in 1985.

fuentes/cronica-de-eponimos-de-mari/por_.texto: It is a source for the chronology of the period: Michel proposed identifying a solar eclipse in the year of the eponym Puzur-Ishtar with the one of 24 June 1833 BC.

fuentes/historia-sincronica/resumen.texto: Assyrian chronicle that recounts, in the form of synchronisms between the kings of both countries, the clashes and border treaties between Assyria and Babylon from Ashur-uballit I onward. It records, among others, the revolt against Kara-hardash, the battle of Sugagu and the battle of Kar-Ishtar of Ugarsallu.

fuentes/historia-sincronica/por_que_impo.texto: It gives the Assyrian version of those conflicts: the Chronicle P recounts some of them differently, such as the battle of Sugagu.

fuentes/relieve-burney/resumen.texto: Terracotta plaque 49,5 cm high showing a winged, naked female figure with bird's talons, flanked by owls and standing on two lions. The British Museum dates it between 1800 and 1750 BC; it comes from southern Mesopotamia, but the exact site is unknown.

fuentes/relieve-burney/por_que_importa.texto: Its authenticity was questioned from the time it appeared in the 1930s, and the date and the identity of the figure are debated, although it is usually accepted that the subject is religious.

personas/ishbi-erra/resumen.texto: Official of the last king of Ur III, Ibbi-Sin, who settled in Isin and founded its first dynasty, which reigned c. 2018-1985 BC (middle chronology). He is credited with expelling the Elamites from Ur; the Sumerian King List gives him 33 years of reign, but only one inscription of his has been found.

personas/shu-ilishu/resumen.texto: Second king of the Isin dynasty, son of Ishbi-Erra, who reigned c. 1985-1975 BC (middle chronology). He wrote his name with the divine determinative and held the title king of Sumer and Akkad.

personas/iddin-dagan/resumen.texto: Third king of Isin, c. 1975-1954 BC (middle chronology), son of Shu-Ilishu. He is known for his part in the sacred marriage rite and for the hymn in his honor that describes him.

personas/ishme-dagan-de-isin/resumen.texto: Fourth king of Isin, c. 1954-1935 BC (middle chronology), son and successor of Iddin-Dagan according to the Sumerian King List. Hymns were written in his honor, in a style that imitates those of Shulgi of Ur III.

personas/lipit-ishtar/resumen.texto: Fifth king of Isin, c. 1935-1924 BC (middle chronology), son of Ishme-Dagan. He is known above all for the hymns in his honor and for the law code that bears his name, a century older than that of Hammurabi.

personas/ur-ninurta/resumen.texto: Sixth king of Isin, c. 1923-1896 BC (middle chronology). He took the throne at the fall of Lipit-Ishtar and held it for some 28 years, until his violent death.

personas/bur-suen/resumen.texto: Seventh king of Isin, c. 1895-1874 BC (middle chronology), son of Ur-Ninurta. His reign alternated control over the religious centers of Nippur and Ur, and he was the only one to number his years.

personas/lipit-enlil/resumen.texto: Eighth king of Isin, c. 1873-1868 BC (middle chronology), son of Bur-Suen. The Sumerian King List and the Ur-Isin king list agree on his name and reign.

personas/erra-imitti/resumen.texto: King of Isin c. 1868-1861 BC (middle chronology), successor of Lipit-Enlil, with whom the relationship is unclear. He was a contemporary and rival of Sumuel and Nur-Adad of Larsa.

personas/enlil-bani/resumen.texto: King of Isin c. 1860-1836 BC (middle chronology). Tradition says he was a gardener chosen by Erra-imitti for the ritual of the substitute king, and that he kept the throne when Erra-imitti died; the historicity of that account is uncertain.

personas/zambiya/resumen.texto: King of Isin c. 1836-1833 BC (middle chronology). He is known above all for having been defeated by Sin-iqisham of Larsa.

personas/iter-pisha/resumen.texto: King of Isin c. 1833-1829 BC (middle chronology); the Sumerian King List gives him four years. The Ur-Isin king list was written in the fourth year of the reign of Damiq-ilishu.

personas/ur-du-kuga/resumen.texto: King of Isin c. 1829-1825 BC (middle chronology), the third of a series of short reigns whose filiation is unknown and whose power covered a small region.

personas/suen-magir/resumen.texto: King of Isin c. 1825-1814 BC (middle chronology), with a reign of about eleven years, father of his successor Damiq-ilishu.

personas/damiq-ilishu/resumen.texto: Last king of Isin, c. 1814-1792 BC (middle chronology), with 23 years of reign according to the Ur-Isin king list. He was defeated first by Sin-muballit of Babylon and then by Rim-Sin I of Larsa.

personas/emisum/resumen.texto: Amorite who ruled Larsa c. 2004-1977 BC (middle chronology); he is considered a possible son of Naplanum.

personas/samium/resumen.texto: Amorite who ruled Larsa c. 1976-1941 BC (middle chronology); his son was Zabaia.

personas/zabaia/resumen.texto: Amorite who ruled Larsa c. 1941-1932 BC (middle chronology), son of Samium. A brick inscription records his reconstruction of the Ebabbar of Larsa.

personas/gungunum/resumen.texto: King of Larsa c. 1932-1906 BC (middle chronology), who became independent of Isin and took Ur, so that Isin lost the trade of the Gulf. His year names record victories over Anshan and Malgium.

personas/abisare/resumen.texto: Amorite king of Larsa c. 1905-1895 BC (middle chronology). The annals of his eleven years record that in his ninth year he defeated the city of Isin.

personas/sumuel/resumen.texto: Amorite king of Larsa c. 1895-1866 BC (middle chronology). His daughter Enshakiag-Nanna was priestess (en) of Nanna in Ur.

personas/nur-adad/resumen.texto: King of Larsa c. 1866-1850 BC (middle chronology), contemporary of Erra-imitti of Isin. Some inscriptions show him with the divine determinative, a sign that he was deified in his lifetime.

personas/sin-iddinam/resumen.texto: King of Larsa c. 1849-1843 BC (middle chronology), son of Nur-Adad and deified throughout his reign. According to an inscription found at that site, he built the walls of Mashkan-shapir.

personas/sin-eribam/resumen.texto: King of Larsa for two years, c. 1843-1841 BC (middle chronology), successor of Sin-iddinam.

personas/sin-iqisham/resumen.texto: King of Larsa c. 1841-1835 BC (middle chronology), son of Sin-eribam and contemporary of Zambiya of Isin, whom he defeated.

personas/silli-adad/resumen.texto: King of Larsa for less than a year, c. 1835-1834 BC (middle chronology); the annals say he was “removed from kingship”.

personas/kudur-mabuk/resumen.texto: Senior official of Larsa with titles such as “father of the Amorite land”, who first appears in Mashkan-shapir under Sin-iddinam. His sons Warad-Sin and Rim-Sin I were kings of Larsa; he himself never reigned.

personas/warad-sin/resumen.texto: King of Larsa c. 1834-1823 BC (middle chronology), son of Kudur-Mabuk, with the titles of governor of Ur and of Lagash. He may have co-reigned with his father.

personas/rim-sin-i/resumen.texto: King of Larsa c. 1822-1763 BC (middle chronology), brother of Warad-Sin, who annexed Isin and Uruk. He was defeated by Hammurabi of Babylon in 1763 BC, with whom he had been allied.

personas/rim-sin-ii/resumen.texto: Last king of Larsa, who rebelled against Samsu-iluna of Babylon c. 1742-1739 BC (middle chronology); he may have been a nephew of Rim-Sin I. His uprising spread to about 26 cities.

personas/anam-de-uruk/resumen.texto: Ruler of Uruk in the Old Babylonian period, with the titles “shepherd of Uruk” and “commander of the army of Uruk”. He was the father of Irdanene.

personas/irdanene/resumen.texto: Ruler of Uruk in the Old Babylonian period, son and successor of An-am and contemporary of Rim-Sin I of Larsa, who captured him in battle.

personas/sin-kashid/resumen.texto: Amorite king of Uruk in the 19th century BC, known for his many inscriptions recording building works; no year names survive, so the length of his reign is uncertain. He married Shallurtum, daughter of Sumu-la-El of Babylon, and was a contemporary of Nur-Adad of Larsa and Enlil-bani of Isin.

personas/ipiq-adad-ii/resumen.texto: King of Eshnunna, son of Ibal-pi-El I. He began with the title ensi and then took the title of king; he greatly expanded the state and laid the foundations of its regional power.

personas/naram-sin-de-eshnunna/resumen.texto: King of Eshnunna for at least nine years, during the period when the kingdom was a political power; he succeeded Ipiq-Adad II.

personas/dadusha/resumen.texto: King of Eshnunna, ally of Shamshi-Adad I around 1781 BC, when they conquered the region between the two Zabs, an event recalled by a victory stela.

personas/ibal-pi-el-ii/resumen.texto: King of Eshnunna c. 1779-1765 BC. He negotiated with Shamshi-Adad I and with Zimri-Lim of Mari.

personas/bilalama/resumen.texto: Ruler of Eshnunna in the 20th century BC, who maintained good relations with Ilum-muttabbil of Der and with Elam. Inscriptions at Eshnunna are attributed to him.

personas/iluni/resumen.texto: King of Eshnunna for between 8 and 20 years at the end of the 18th century BC, in diplomatic contact with Elam. Samsu-iluna defeated him and had him executed in Babylon.

personas/sumu-abum/resumen.texto: First king of the first dynasty of Babylon, c. 1894-1881 BC (middle chronology). He freed a small region previously dominated by Kazallu, which included Babylon, then a minor administrative center.

personas/sumu-la-el/resumen.texto: King of Babylon c. 1881-1845 BC (middle chronology), who conquered Kish and Sippar and fortified his territory. He married his daughter Shallurtum to Sin-kashid of Uruk.

personas/sabium/resumen.texto: Amorite king of the first dynasty of Babylon, c. 1844-1831 BC (middle chronology), at the head of a small and recent kingdom that included Babylon. He did not claim the broad titles of kingship.

personas/apil-sin/resumen.texto: King of Babylon c. 1830-1813 BC (middle chronology) and grandfather of Hammurabi. In his time Babylon was becoming a local kingdom.

personas/sin-muballit/resumen.texto: King of Babylon c. 1812-1793 BC (middle chronology), father of Hammurabi. He was the first ruler of Babylon to declare himself king in the broad sense.

personas/samsu-iluna/resumen.texto: Son and successor of Hammurabi, king c. 1749-1712 BC (middle chronology). He had to face rebellions in the territories conquered by his father, the abandonment of several southern cities, and the independence of the Sealand.

personas/abi-eshuh/resumen.texto: Eighth king of the first dynasty of Babylon, c. 1711-1684 BC (middle chronology), son of Samsu-iluna.

personas/ammi-ditana/resumen.texto: King of Babylon c. 1683-1647 BC (middle chronology), son of Abi-eshuh. The names of his first 37 years of reign are preserved.

personas/ammi-saduqa/resumen.texto: King of Babylon c. 1646-1626 BC (middle chronology). His reign gives its name to the Venus tablet, an astronomical record attributed to him through its original compilation.

personas/samsu-ditana/resumen.texto: Eleventh and last king of the first dynasty of Babylon, c. 1625-1595 BC (middle chronology). He was defeated by the Hittite king Mursili I, who carried off the statue of Marduk.

personas/gulkishar/resumen.texto: Sixth king of the first dynasty of the Sealand, around 1595 BC, contemporary with the end of the reign of Samsu-ditana. He was the subject of a royal epic about his enmity with Samsu-ditana.

personas/peshgaldaramesh/resumen.texto: Eighth king of the Sealand, c. 1534-1485 BC, with a speculative date: the chronologies of the dynasty do not fit, because the Assyrian Synchronistic King List pairs him with Bazaya (c. 1649-1622 BC) and his predecessor Gulkishar is contemporary with Samsu-ditana, down to c. 1595. He is known from the royal lists, from later Babylonian chronicles and from some 470 texts of the Schøyen collection, from a clandestine excavation of an unknown site; the lists give him 50 years, but his year names reach only year 29.

personas/ulamburiash/resumen.texto: Kassite king who conquered the Sealand by defeating Ea-gamil, the last king of the first dynasty of the Sealand, and thereby reunified Babylonia, around 1475 BC.

personas/agum-ii/resumen.texto: Agum II or Agum-kakrime, Kassite king with no secure place in the list, probably the ninth of the dynasty, after the Hittite sack of Babylon.

personas/burna-buriash-i/resumen.texto: First Kassite to rule Babylonia securely, perhaps the first to occupy the city of Babylon around 1500 BC.

personas/kashtiliash-iii/resumen.texto: Kassite king of Babylon in the 15th century BC, brother of Ulamburiash according to the Chronicle of the Ancient Kings. He is also known from the Assyrian Synchronistic King List, from a copy of a monumental inscription about the digging of the Sumundar canal, and from his genealogy as son of Burna-Buriash I.

personas/agum-iii/resumen.texto: Kassite king of Babylon, of uncertain place in the list (possibly the thirteenth), who died around 1440 BC.

personas/karaindash/resumen.texto: Kassite king of the late 15th century BC, with the title “king of Sumer and Akkad”. He had a small temple of original decoration built in Eanna, the complex at Uruk.

personas/kadashman-harbe-i/resumen.texto: Sixteenth Kassite king of Babylon, c. 1400-1388 BC, approximately.

personas/kurigalzu-i/resumen.texto: Kassite king from c. 1387 to c. 1375 BC, with a very approximate date. He promoted a broad building program and founded Dur-Kurigalzu.

personas/kadashman-enlil-i/resumen.texto: Kassite king of Babylon c. 1375-1360 BC, who corresponded with the pharaoh Amenhotep III (EA 1 to EA 5).

personas/burna-buriash-ii/resumen.texto: Kassite king of Babylon c. 1359-1333 BC, of the Late Bronze Age. He corresponded with Egypt and married a daughter to a Hittite king.

personas/kara-hardash/resumen.texto: King of Babylon around 1333 BC, possibly a son of Burna-Buriash II, whose reign was brief and ended with his death.

personas/kurigalzu-ii/resumen.texto: Kassite king of Babylon c. 1332-1308 BC, son of Burna-Buriash II. He was placed on the throne by Ashur-uballit I of Assyria and later turned against him.

personas/nazi-maruttash/resumen.texto: Kassite king of Babylon c. 1307-1282 BC, who proclaimed himself “king of the world”. He is mentioned in Ludlul bel nemeqi.

personas/kadashman-turgu/resumen.texto: Kassite king of Babylon c. 1281-1264 BC, son of Nazi-Maruttash.

personas/kadashman-enlil-ii/resumen.texto: Kassite king of Babylon c. 1263-1255 BC, son of Kadashman-Turgu.

personas/kudur-enlil/resumen.texto: Kassite king of Babylon c. 1254-1246 BC. He reached his ninth regnal year according to contemporary economic tablets.

personas/shagarakti-shuriash/resumen.texto: Kassite king of Babylon c. 1245-1233 BC, who carried out major works at Nippur together with Kadashman-Enlil and Kudur-Enlil.

personas/kashtiliash-iv/resumen.texto: Kassite king of Babylon c. 1232-1225 BC. He went to war with Assyria and was defeated by Tukulti-Ninurta I, who invaded Babylon.

personas/enlil-nadin-shumi/resumen.texto: King of Babylon around 1224 BC, placed on the throne after the fall of Kashtiliash IV to Tukulti-Ninurta I.

personas/kadashman-harbe-ii/resumen.texto: Kassite king of Babylon around 1223 BC, successor of Enlil-nadin-shumi, with a brief reign.

personas/adad-shuma-iddina/resumen.texto: Kassite king of Babylon c. 1222-1217 BC, with six years of reign.

personas/adad-shuma-usur/resumen.texto: Kassite king of Babylon c. 1216-1187 BC (very tentative dates), with a thoroughly Babylonian name.

personas/meli-shipak-ii/resumen.texto: Kassite king of Babylon c. 1186-1172 BC, with 15 years of reign. His reign is a key synchronism in the chronology of the ancient Near East.

personas/marduk-apla-iddina-i/resumen.texto: Kassite king of Babylon c. 1171-1159 BC, son of Meli-Shipak II.

personas/enlil-nadin-ahi/resumen.texto: Last Kassite king of Babylon, c. 1157-1155 BC. According to later chronicles, he was defeated by Kutir-Nahhunte of Elam, who deported him to Susa with the Kassite nobles and the statue of Marduk.

personas/puzur-ashur-i/resumen.texto: Considered the founder of Assyria as an independent state, c. 2025 BC (middle chronology). He reigned in the 21st century BC after the collapse of the Ur III empire.

personas/shalim-ahum/resumen.texto: Ruler of Assur at the end of the 21st and beginning of the 20th century BC; in his only known inscription he is called son of Puzur-Ashur I, and he is the earliest attested independent ruler in a contemporary text.

personas/ilu-shuma/resumen.texto: Son of Shalim-ahum and ruler of Assur at the beginning of the 20th century BC, who died around 1975 BC.

personas/erishum-i/resumen.texto: Son of Ilu-shuma, ruler of Assur c. 1974-1935 BC according to the royal list; he is the first of the rulers of Assur from whom many inscriptions survive, and the period of trade with Kanesh.

personas/ikunum/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1935-1921 BC (middle chronology).

personas/sargon-i-de-asiria/resumen.texto: Ruler of Assur c. 1921-1881 BC (middle chronology), with the title “steward of Assur”.

personas/puzur-ashur-ii/resumen.texto: Ruler of Assur c. 1881-1873 BC, son and successor of Sargon I.

personas/naram-sin-de-asiria/resumen.texto: Ruler of Assur, with the title “steward of Assur”, who reigned until c. 1823 BC according to the Assyrian list in its variants.

personas/erishum-ii/resumen.texto: Son and successor of Naram-Sin, ruler of Assur until c. 1809 BC, when Shamshi-Adad I displaced him.

personas/ila-kabkabu/resumen.texto: Amorite king, father of Shamshi-Adad I according to the Assyrian King List; he clashed with Yaggid-Lim of Mari. The sources differ about his seat: some make him king of Terqa and others of Ekallatum.

personas/shamshi-adad-i/resumen.texto: Amorite ruler of Ekallatum who conquered Assur and founded the Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia, c. 1809-1776 BC (middle chronology). He made Shubat-Enlil his capital and placed his sons in charge of Mari and Ekallatum.

personas/ishme-dagan-i/resumen.texto: Son of Shamshi-Adad I, who ruled Ekallatum and Assur. The Assyrian list gives him 40 years of reign, but his actual reign was shorter and ended c. 1765 BC.

personas/yasmah-adad/resumen.texto: Youngest son of Shamshi-Adad I, installed on the throne of Mari by his father. He was expelled by Zimri-Lim after the death of Shamshi-Adad.

personas/mut-ashkur/resumen.texto: Hurrian name known only from a mention in the Assyrian King List as a possible son of Ishme-Dagan I; possibly mythical.

personas/rimush-de-asiria/resumen.texto: Possible ruler of Assyria, or of the part centered on Ekallatum, successor of Ishme-Dagan I, who appears only in a variant of the royal list.

personas/asinum/resumen.texto: Grandson of Shamshi-Adad I. He was overthrown by Puzur-Sin because of his Amorite origin, and he is named in the inscriptions of Puzur-Sin but not in the standard list.

personas/puzur-sin/resumen.texto: Assyrian king of the Old Assyrian period, c. 1735 BC, who overthrew Asinum.

personas/ashur-dugul/resumen.texto: King of Assyria in the 18th century BC, during a period of confusion, who reigned six years according to the royal list.

personas/bel-bani/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1700-1691 BC, first ruler of the Adasid dynasty, which governed Assyria for centuries.

personas/libaya/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1690-1674 BC, successor of Bel-bani in the Adasid dynasty.

personas/sharma-adad-i/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1673-1662 BC, son of Libaya and father of Iptar-Sin.

personas/iptar-sin/resumen.texto: Fifty-first king of the Assyrian royal list, with twelve years of reign in the 17th century BC.

personas/bazaya/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1649-1622 BC, number 52 of the royal list, which makes him the successor of Iptar-Sin.

personas/lullaya/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1621-1616 BC, “son of nobody” according to the royal list, that is, without kinship to an earlier king.

personas/shu-ninua/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1615-1602 BC, number 54 of the list, son of his predecessor's predecessor.

personas/shamshi-adad-ii/resumen.texto: Old Assyrian king c. 1585-1580 BC, in a dark period of Assyrian history from which few records survive.

personas/ishme-dagan-ii/resumen.texto: Little-known ruler of Assyria during the first half of the 16th century BC, in a dark age.

personas/shamshi-adad-iii/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1563-1548 BC, son of Ishme-Dagan II, known from an inscription in which he says he repaired two ziggurats.

personas/ashur-nirari-i/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1547-1522 BC, with 26 years of reign, number 60 of the royal list.

personas/puzur-ashur-iii/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1521-1498 BC, son and successor of Ashur-nirari I; the list gives him 24 years or, in another copy, 14.

personas/enlil-nasir-i/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1497-1485 BC, number 62 of the royal list, son of Puzur-Ashur III.

personas/nur-ili/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1484-1473 BC, son of Enlil-nasir I and last king of an independent Assyria before the domination of Mitanni.

personas/ashur-shaduni/resumen.texto: Ruled Assyria for barely a month in the 15th century BC. He was deposed in a coup by Ashur-rabi I.

personas/ashur-rabi-i/resumen.texto: King of Assyria in the 15th century BC. Son of Enlil-nasir I, he took the throne after a coup against Ashur-shaduni.

personas/ashur-nadin-ahhe-i/resumen.texto: King of Assyria in the 15th century BC, son of Ashur-rabi I. During his reign Assyria was occasionally a vassal of Mitanni.

personas/enlil-nasir-ii/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1430-1425 BC, brother of Ashur-nadin-ahhe I, whom he replaced in a coup.

personas/ashur-nirari-ii/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1424-1418 BC, number 68 of the royal list.

personas/ashur-bel-nisheshu/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1417-1409 BC (another dating proposes 1407-1398).

personas/ashur-rim-nisheshu/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1408-1401 BC, with the title “viceroy of Assur”.

personas/eriba-adad-i/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1391-1364 BC. He broke half a century of Hurro-Mitannian influence and was the father of Ashur-uballit I.

personas/ashur-uballit-i/roles.1.texto: founder of the Middle Assyrian Empire

personas/ashur-uballit-i/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1363-1328 BC and first ruler of the Middle Assyrian Empire. He defeated the Mitannian king Shuttarna III and placed Kurigalzu II on the throne of Babylon.

personas/enlil-nirari/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1327-1318 BC, son of Ashur-uballit I.

personas/arik-den-ili/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1317-1306 BC, son of Enlil-nirari, in the Middle Assyrian Empire.

personas/adad-nirari-i/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1305-1274 BC (middle chronology), with more detailed surviving annals than those of his predecessors. He won victories that secured Assyria's position over Hanigalbat.

personas/shalmaneser-i/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1273-1244 BC, son and successor of Adad-nirari I.

personas/tukulti-ninurta-i/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1243-1207 BC, the first known to use the title “king of kings”. He defeated Kashtiliash IV of Babylon, founded Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta and was murdered around 1207 BC.

personas/ashur-nadin-apli/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1206-1203 BC (other dating: 1196-1193), after the death of Tukulti-Ninurta I.

personas/ashur-nirari-iii/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1202-1197 BC, grandson of Tukulti-Ninurta I.

personas/enlil-kudurri-usur/resumen.texto: King of Assyria, number 81 of the royal list, c. 1196-1192 BC.

personas/ninurta-apal-ekur/resumen.texto: Usurper who ruled Assyria c. 1191-1179 BC and styled himself king of the universe and priest of the god Ashur.

personas/ashur-dan-i/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1178-1133 BC (with a variant of 36 years), number 83 of the royal list, son of Ninurta-apal-Ekur.

personas/ninurta-tukulti-ashur/resumen.texto: King of Assyria briefly c. 1132 BC, number 84 of the royal list.

personas/mutakkil-nusku/resumen.texto: King of Assyria briefly c. 1132 BC during a period of political decline.

personas/ashur-resh-ishi-i/resumen.texto: King of Assyria 1132-1115 BC, son of Mutakkil-Nusku, number 86 of the royal list.

personas/tiglatpileser-i/resumen.texto: King of Assyria 1114-1076 BC. He ruled the Middle Assyrian Empire after Ashur-resh-ishi I.

personas/yaggid-lim/resumen.texto: King of Mari in the 19th century BC, probably Amorite; he clashed with Ila-kabkabu of Terqa.

personas/yahdun-lim/resumen.texto: King of Mari, Tuttul and the land of Hana, who died around 1797 BC.

personas/zimri-lim/resumen.texto: Last king of Mari, c. 1775-1761 BC. His reign is among the best documented of antiquity thanks to the palace archives; Hammurabi destroyed Mari in 1761 BC.

personas/shibtu/resumen.texto: Chief wife of Zimri-Lim and queen of Mari, princess of Yamhad (Aleppo). She married Zimri-Lim in the second year of his reign.

personas/atamrum/resumen.texto: King of Andarig and later also of Allahad, an ally of Elam and active in the negotiations with Mari.

personas/muballitat-sherua/resumen.texto: Princess of Assyria, daughter of Ashur-uballit I, who married the Kassite king Burna-Buriash II; their son was Kara-hardash.

personas/zababa-shuma-iddin/resumen.texto: Penultimate king of the Kassite dynasty of Babylon, who reigned a single year, c. 1158 BC (middle chronology). He had no apparent ties to the royal family, and the circumstances of his accession are not known; Shutruk-Nahhunte of Elam deposed him in his invasion of Babylon.

personas/marduk-kabit-ahheshu/roles.1.texto: founder of the Second Dynasty of Isin

personas/marduk-kabit-ahheshu/resumen.texto: Founder of the Second Dynasty of Isin, who governed Babylon until c. 1022 BC. He reigned c. 1153-1136 BC (middle chronology), 18 years according to Babylonian King List C, and came to the throne after the Elamite fall of the Kassite dynasty.

personas/mursili-i/resumen.texto: King of the Hittites c. 1620-1590 BC (middle chronology), probably grandson of Hattusili I. He sacked Babylon around 1595 BC, ending the first dynasty of Babylon.

personas/shutruk-nahhunte/resumen.texto: King of Elam c. 1184-1155 BC (middle chronology) and first king of the Shutrukid dynasty. He invaded Kassite Babylon in 1158 BC and carried off monuments from Babylon, Sippar and Eshnunna to Susa, among them the stele of Naram-Sin, to which he added an Elamite inscription; he also deposed Zababa-shuma-iddin. He is believed to have been married to a daughter of the Kassite king Meli-Shipak II.

personas/kidin-hutran/resumen.texto: Elamite king of the Igihalkid dynasty known for his wars with Babylon. The Chronicle P describes two attacks: in the first he crossed the Tigris, sacked Der and Nippur, and deposed King Enlil-nadin-shumi; in the second, under Adad-shuma-iddina, he attacked Marad and Isin. A Berlin letter presents him as the son of Untash-Napirisha and of a daughter of Burna-Buriash.

personas/untash-napirisha/resumen.texto: King of Elam around 1300 BC, son of Humban-Numena and of a daughter or granddaughter of Kurigalzu. He founded Dur-Untash (Chogha Zanbil), with its ziggurat, and dedicated a statue to his father-in-law, the Babylonian king Burna-Buriash; if this was Burna-Buriash II, his reign falls in the mid-14th century BC.

personas/siwe-palar-huppak/resumen.texto: Grand regent (sukkalmah) of Elam from c. 1778 to c. 1745 BC. He was actively involved in Mesopotamian politics and maintained relations with Babylon. He died around 1745 BC.

personas/sin-leqi-unninni/resumen.texto: Exorcist who probably lived between 1300 and 1000 BC; his date is uncertain. Tradition credits him with the best-preserved version of the Gilgamesh epic, the one with the incipit “ša nagba īmuru”, in which his name appears, something unusual in cuneiform texts. Andrew George argues that he gave it its final and fixed form; how much he changed the earlier versions is not known.

personas/esagil-kin-apli/resumen.texto: Chief of the scholars (ummanu) of the Babylonian king Adad-apla-iddina, who reigned 1067-1046 BC and came from Borsippa. He is the author of the Diagnostic Handbook (Sakikku), a medical treatise that deduces the cause, often supernatural, and the prognosis from the symptoms. His activity falls shortly after the end of the Kassite dynasty.

personas/addu-duri/resumen.texto: Senior official in the reign of Zimri-Lim at Mari, possibly the queen mother, who died around 1768 BC.

personas/iltani/resumen.texto: Wife of Aqba-hammu, ruler of Karana, and daughter of King Samu-Addu of Karana, around 1750 BC. Her archive, found at Tell al-Rimah, contains some 200 letters and administrative records on the management of the palace's textile and food industries, in which 15 women and 10 men worked.

personas/ea-nasir/resumen.texto: Copper merchant of Ur, to whom a dissatisfied customer addressed the complaint tablet UET V 81 around 1750 BC; Leonard Woolley found it at Ur.

personas/yarim-lim-i/resumen.texto: Second king of the Amorite kingdom of Yamhad, with its capital at Aleppo, died c. 1764 BC. Zimri-Lim of Mari called him “father” and married his daughter Shibtu.

personas/shattuara-i/resumen.texto: Hurrian king of Mitanni c. 1305-1285 BC. An inscription of Adad-nirari I of Assyria says that he rebelled against his Assyrian lord, was captured, and that his oath of loyalty was renewed.

personas/shattuara-ii/resumen.texto: Last known king of Mitanni (Hanigalbat) in the 13th century BC, before the Assyrian conquest. An Assyrian inscription says that a king Shattuara of Hanigalbat made war on Shalmaneser I; it is possible that the account recalls the rebellion against Adad-nirari I.

personas/kutir-nahhunte/resumen.texto: Son of Shutruk-Nahhunte of Elam, whom his father left in command of Babylon after the invasion of c. 1158 BC. According to later Babylonian texts, he defeated Enlil-nadin-ahi and deported him to Susa with the Kassite nobles and the statue of Marduk, an act for which Babylonian tradition blamed him.

personas/nazi-bugash/resumen.texto: Kassite (also called Shuzigash) whom the army placed on the throne of Babylon after the murder of Kara-hardash in an anti-Assyrian revolt, c. 1333 BC. Ashur-uballit I of Assyria, grandfather of Kara-hardash, deposed him and put Kurigalzu II in his place.

personas/ilum-ma-ili/resumen.texto: Founder of the first dynasty of the Sealand, contemporary of Samsu-iluna and of Abi-eshuh of Babylon; the royal list gives him 60 years of reign. Only the year of his accession and the following year are known of him, and his date (c. 1725 BC) is very speculative.

personas/itti-ili-nibi/resumen.texto: Second king of the first dynasty of the Sealand, with 56 years of reign according to the royal lists. Only a later chronicle (the Babylonian King List B) mentions him, with no other reference; his date is very uncertain.

personas/damqi-ilishu-ii/resumen.texto: Third king of the first dynasty of the Sealand, with 36 years of reign according to the lists. A letter from the Babylonian fortress of Dur-Abi-eshuh, from the time of Ammi-ditana, mentions news about a Damqi-ilishu; his date is very uncertain.

personas/ishkibal/resumen.texto: Fourth king of the first dynasty of the Sealand, with 15 years of reign according to the royal lists. The Assyrian Synchronistic King List pairs him with Bel-bani; his date is very uncertain.

personas/shushushi/resumen.texto: Fifth king of the first dynasty of the Sealand, with 24 years of reign according to the royal lists. The Assyrian Synchronistic King List pairs him with Libaya; his date is very uncertain.

personas/ayadaragalama/resumen.texto: King of the Sealand, descendant of Peshgaldaramesh, with 28 years of reign according to the lists. His year names recall that he expelled “two enemies”, perhaps Elamites and Kassites, and that he raised a “great ring against the Kassite enemy”; the archive of Tell Khaiber dates from his reign. His date is very uncertain.

personas/akurduana/resumen.texto: King of the Sealand with 26 years of reign according to the lists, successor of Ayadaragalama. Only later chronicles name him; his date is very uncertain.

personas/melamkurkurra/resumen.texto: King of the Sealand with 7 years of reign according to the lists, successor of Akurduana. Only later chronicles name him; his date is very uncertain.

personas/ea-gamil/resumen.texto: Last king of the first dynasty of the Sealand, with 9 years of reign according to the lists. The Kassite king Ulamburiash defeated him around 1475 BC.

personas/gandash/roles.0.texto: first king of the Kassite dynasty according to the lists

personas/gandash/resumen.texto: First king of the Kassite dynasty in the later royal lists, with 26 years of reign; reconstructions of the lists place him c. 1729-1704 BC, but it is probable that the first kings of the series did not reign in Babylon. A school copy from the first millennium of an alleged inscription of his presents him as king of Sumer and Akkad and of Babylon.

personas/agum-i/roles.0.texto: Kassite king according to the lists

personas/agum-i/resumen.texto: Second king of the Kassite dynasty in the lists, with 22 years of reign, son of Gandash; the inscription of Agum-kakrime cites him among the ancestors of that king with the epithet “the great”. He is known only from later lists.

personas/kashtiliash-i/roles.0.texto: Kassite king according to the lists

personas/kashtiliash-i/resumen.texto: Third king of the Kassite dynasty in the lists, with 22 years of reign, son of Agum I. He is known only from later lists and from the inscription of Agum-kakrime, which cites him among the ancestors of that king.

personas/abi-rattash/roles.0.texto: Kassite king according to the lists

personas/abi-rattash/resumen.texto: Kassite king of the series before the Hittite sack, with no surviving length of reign. The inscription of Agum-kakrime cites him as an ancestor of that king (“the fierce hero”); the lists are damaged and contradict one another about his place.

personas/kashtiliash-ii/roles.0.texto: Kassite king according to the lists

personas/kashtiliash-ii/resumen.texto: Kassite king who appears only in the Assyrian Synchronistic King List, between Abi-Rattash and Urzigurumash, with no surviving length of reign; List A of the Babylonian kings does not include him.

personas/urzigurumash/roles.0.texto: Kassite king according to the lists

personas/urzigurumash/resumen.texto: Kassite king with no surviving length of reign, descendant of Abi-Rattash and father of Agum II according to the latter's inscription. He is known only from later lists and from that inscription.

personas/harba-shipak/roles.0.texto: Kassite king according to the lists

personas/harba-shipak/resumen.texto: Kassite king of the series before Burna-Buriash I, with no surviving length of reign; his name appears in the Assyrian Synchronistic King List with a partial reading.

personas/shiptaulzi/activo.lugar.texto: Babylon (according to tablets from Tell Muhammad)

personas/shiptaulzi/resumen.texto: Kassite king of the series before Burna-Buriash I. A date formula on the tablets from Tell Muhammad mentions “the year of King Shipta'ulzi” and the resettlement of Babylon.

personas/ashur-apla-idi/resumen.texto: First of the five rulers whom the Assyrian King List makes rivals of Ashur-dugul, whose joint reign could not have exceeded one year. Some doubt that any of them reigned in his own right: the sequence of names resembles that of the eponyms of Ashur-dugul's reign.

personas/nasir-sin/resumen.texto: One of the five rivals of Ashur-dugul mentioned in the Assyrian King List, with no other information; some Assyriologists doubt that he reigned.

personas/sin-namir/resumen.texto: One of the five rivals of Ashur-dugul mentioned in the Assyrian King List, with no other information; some Assyriologists doubt that he reigned.

personas/ipqi-ishtar/resumen.texto: One of the five rivals of Ashur-dugul mentioned in the Assyrian King List, with no other information; some Assyriologists doubt that he reigned.

personas/adad-salulu/resumen.texto: Last of the five rivals of Ashur-dugul mentioned in the Assyrian King List, with no other information; some Assyriologists doubt that he reigned.

personas/adasi/resumen.texto: Father of Bel-bani. The Assyrian King List counts him among the rulers unrelated to the earlier kings, and the Adasid dynasty takes its name from him.

personas/sharma-adad-ii/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1601-1599 BC, with three years of reign, son of Shu-Ninua and brother of his successor Erishum III.

personas/erishum-iii/resumen.texto: King of Assyria c. 1598-1586 BC, with 13 years of reign, son of Shu-Ninua and father of Shamshi-Adad II.

personas/babu-aha-iddina/roles.0.texto: chancellor and chief of the royal storehouse

personas/babu-aha-iddina/resumen.texto: High Assyrian official who served under Adad-nirari I, Shalmaneser I and Tukulti-Ninurta I, c. 1279-1239 BC. His archive of 49 tablets and fragments, found at Assur, records the trade in raw materials and ivory; drafts of letters from Hattusa may be addressed to him.

personas/ili-pada/roles.0.texto: grand vizier of Assyria and king of Hanigalbat

personas/ili-pada/resumen.texto: Member of a collateral branch of the Assyrian royal family who was grand vizier of Assyria and king of the dependent state of Hanigalbat around 1200 BC, in the time of Ashur-nirari III. The fortress of Tell Sabi Abyad was his country estate, and he was the father of the future king Ninurta-apal-Ekur.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-dinastia-de-isin/.texto: Ishbi-Erra Founds the Dynasty of Isin

Ishbi-Erra, an official of the last king of Ur III, Ibbi-Sin, settles in Isin and founds the first dynasty of that city, which presented itself as the successor of Ur III (c. 2018 BC in the middle chronology; the short and long chronologies move it by decades). The Sumerian King List says that kingship passed to Isin after the fall of Ur.

hechos/isin-expulsa-a-los-elamitas-de-ur.texto: Ishbi-Erra Expels the Elamites from Ur

A year name of Ishbi-Erra celebrates that he drove out of Ur, with his mighty weapon, the Elamite who lived among its people. The exact date is unknown, but it is placed at the beginning of his reign, after the fall of Ur III.

hechos/larsa-independiente-de-isin-y-cap.texto: Gungunum of Larsa Breaks Away from Isin and Takes Ur

Gungunum, who ruled Larsa c. 1932-1906 BC, became independent of Isin and took Ur, the center of Persian Gulf trade, so that Isin lost that source of wealth. The exact date of the taking of Ur within his reign is uncertain.

hechos/promulgacion-del-codigo-de-lipit-.texto: King Lipit-Ishtar of Isin has a legal collection that bears his name drawn up in Sumerian, a century older than the code of Hammurabi and copied in scribal education for centuries.

hechos/promulgacion-de-las-leyes-de-eshn.texto: The tablets found at Tell Harmal are copies of a law collection from c. 1930 BC of the kingdom of Eshnunna. They differ from the code of Hammurabi, among other things, in that they are not attributed to a king.

hechos/abisare-de-larsa-derrota-a-isin/t.texto: Abisare of Larsa Defeats the City of Isin

hechos/abisare-de-larsa-derrota-a-isin/r.texto: The annals of Abisare of Larsa record that in his ninth regnal year he defeated the city of Isin. It belongs to the rivalry between Larsa and Isin over canals and over Nippur.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-primera-dinastia-.texto: Sumu-abum Founds the First Dynasty of Babylon

Sumu-abum, an Amorite, settles in small Babylon, then a minor administrative center freed from the domination of Kazallu, and founds the first Babylonian dynasty (c. 1894 BC in the middle chronology). Neither he nor his three successors styled themselves kings of Babylon.

hechos/sumu-la-el-conquista-kish-y-sippa.texto: Sumu-la-El of Babylon Conquers Kish and Sippar

Sumu-la-El, king of Babylon c. 1881-1845 BC, subjugates neighboring cities such as Kish and Sippar and builds a chain of fortresses around his territory. The date of each conquest within his reign is uncertain.

hechos/matrimonio-de-sin-kashid-y-shallu.texto: Marriage of Sin-kashid of Uruk to the Daughter of Sumu-la-El
Sin-kashid, Amorite king of Uruk, married Shallurtum, daughter of Sumu-la-El of Babylon, in a diplomatic marriage between the two dynasties.

hechos/sin-iddinam-ataca-eshnunna/resume.texto: A year name of Sin-iddinam of Larsa recalls that “the land of Eshnunna was destroyed”. Sin-iddinam also concluded a treaty with Ibal-pi-El I of Eshnunna and Sin-kashid of Uruk against Sabium of Babylon.

hechos/alianza-de-eshnunna-larsa-y-uruk/.texto: Treaty of Eshnunna, Larsa and Uruk against Babylon

Ibal-pi-El I of Eshnunna concluded a treaty with Sin-iddinam of Larsa and Sin-kashid of Uruk against Sabium of Babylon and Ikun-pi-Sin of Nerebtum. An Old Babylonian letter says that Nerebtum would not give troops to either side.

hechos/enlil-bani-y-el-rey-sustituto/tit.texto: Enlil-bani Accedes to the Throne of Isin

hechos/enlil-bani-y-el-rey-sustituto/res.texto: The Chronicle of the Ancient Kings relates that Erra-imitti appointed Enlil-bani, his gardener, as substitute king in a ritual, and that when Erra-imitti died in his palace while eating hot porridge, Enlil-bani did not abdicate and went on reigning; the historicity of the account is uncertain.

hechos/rim-sin-i-captura-kisurra/titulo.texto: Rim-Sin I of Larsa Takes Kisurra

hechos/rim-sin-i-captura-kisurra/resumen.texto: Rim-Sin I claims to have captured Kisurra in his twentieth regnal year. Texts and excavations show the decline of the city in the time of Hammurabi.

hechos/rim-sin-i-derrota-a-la-coalicion-.texto: Rim-Sin I Defeats the Coalition of Uruk, Isin and Babylon
According to a year name and three inscriptions, Rim-Sin I defeated the army of Uruk, Isin, Babylon, Rapiqum and Sutium and captured Irdanene, king of Uruk.

hechos/rim-sin-i-anexa-isin/titulo.texto: Rim-Sin I of Larsa Annexes Isin

hechos/rim-sin-i-anexa-isin/resumen.texto: Isin kept its independence from Larsa for some forty years more and ended up subjected to Rim-Sin I. The exact date of the annexation is not known.

hechos/hammurabi-toma-isin-y-uruk/resume.texto: The seventh year of Hammurabi commemorates the capture of Isin and Uruk, cities of Larsa. It was a short raid, because both cities returned to Larsa's hands.

hechos/fundacion-de-shubat-enlil/titulo.texto: Shamshi-Adad I Turns Shekhna into Shubat-Enlil

hechos/fundacion-de-shubat-enlil/resumen.texto: Shamshi-Adad I occupies the former, abandoned Shekhna and, around 1808-1800 BC, makes it his capital under the name Shubat-Enlil, “residence of the god Enlil”.

hechos/reino-de-la-alta-mesopotamia/titu.texto: Shamshi-Adad I Creates the Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia

hechos/reino-de-la-alta-mesopotamia/resu.texto: Shamshi-Adad I, of Ekallatum, conquers Assur and Upper Mesopotamia and comes to control the largest territory between the Tigris and the Euphrates since Ur III. He placed his son Yasmah-Adad at Mari and Ishme-Dagan at Ekallatum; this kingdom is known from texts from Mari, Chagar Bazar, Tuttul and Shemshara.

hechos/shamshi-adad-conquista-assur/resu.texto: Around 1809 BC Shamshi-Adad I deposes Erishum II, son of Naram-Sin, and takes Assur. The Assyrian King List counts him among the kings of Assyria and, according to tradition, his son Ishme-Dagan I governed it as part of his father's kingdom.

hechos/yasmah-adad-en-el-trono-de-mari/t.texto: Shamshi-Adad I Places His Son Yasmah-Adad on the Throne of Mari

hechos/yasmah-adad-en-el-trono-de-mari/r.texto: Shamshi-Adad I displaced the family of Yahdun-Lim and put his youngest son, Yasmah-Adad, on the throne of Mari. The members of the deposed family took refuge in Aleppo. The exact date of the taking of Mari is not known.

hechos/dadusha-y-shamshi-adad-conquistan.texto: Dadusha of Eshnunna and Shamshi-Adad I Conquer the Region between the Two Zabs

A victory stela records that around 1781 BC Dadusha of Eshnunna and Shamshi-Adad I, as allies, conquered the region between the two rivers Zab, and that Dadusha handed the lands over to Shamshi-Adad I.

hechos/muerte-de-shamshi-adad-i/titulo.texto: Death of Shamshi-Adad I and Fall of His Kingdom

hechos/muerte-de-shamshi-adad-i/resumen.texto: Shamshi-Adad I dies around 1776 BC and his kingdom disintegrates: Eshnunna takes cities around Assur, Zimri-Lim expels Yasmah-Adad from Mari, and the rest was lost later under Ishme-Dagan I, first to a coalition of Mari, Andarig and Eshnunna and then to Hammurabi.

hechos/zimri-lim-recupera-mari/titulo.texto: Zimri-Lim Recovers the Throne of Mari

hechos/zimri-lim-recupera-mari/resumen.texto: After the death of Shamshi-Adad I, Zimri-Lim, of the family of Yahdun-Lim and exiled in Aleppo, returns to Mari, expels Yasmah-Adad and becomes king (c. 1775-1761 BC).

hechos/matrimonio-de-zimri-lim-y-shibtu/.texto: In his second regnal year Zimri-Lim married Shibtu, princess of Yamhad (Aleppo). In practice she was his first wife and held a central place in the administration of the palace.

hechos/zimri-lim-vence-a-los-benjaminita.texto: The third year of Zimri-Lim commemorates his victory over the Benjaminites, a rival tribal confederation. His reign knew peace only between the sixth and ninth years.

hechos/hammurabi-destruye-larsa/titulo.texto: Hammurabi Defeats Rim-Sin I and Annexes Larsa

hechos/hammurabi-destruye-larsa/resumen.texto: Hammurabi, with the help of Zimri-Lim, attacks his former ally Rim-Sin I of Larsa, defeats him and annexes his kingdom in 1763 BC. With this he dominates the whole lower plain of Mesopotamia.

hechos/hammurabi-ocupa-eshnunna/resumen.texto: The Babylonians occupied Eshnunna in year 31 of Hammurabi (1762 BC). The name of his year 32 recalls a victory over that kingdom and over Shubartum and Gutium.

hechos/destruccion-de-mari-por-hammurabi.texto: Hammurabi broke with Zimri-Lim, his former ally, and occupied Mari in 1761 BC for a few months: he emptied the palace of almost all its contents, sorted the archives and took to Babylon whatever interested him. When the occupation ended, in 1759 BC, he destroyed the city and its palace systematically, as reconstructed from the year names; with that, the Mari archives come to an end.

hechos/canal-de-hammurabi/titulo.texto: Hammurabi Digs the Canal “Hammurabi Brings Abundance to the People”

hechos/canal-de-hammurabi/resumen.texto: Year 33 of Hammurabi commemorates the completion of a canal in the south of his kingdom, bearing that name, and also recalls the restoration of Sumer and Akkad and the submission of Mari and Malgium.

hechos/eshnunna-inundada-bajo-hammurabi/.texto: According to Charpin, the name of year 38 of Hammurabi mentions a flood that destroyed Eshnunna, already very weakened; a change in the course of the Diyala led to its abandonment. It is a disputed interpretation.

hechos/promulgacion-del-codigo-de-hammur.texto: The Code of Hammurabi Is Drafted
The prologue of the Code of Hammurabi, dated toward the end of his reign, lists the cities under Babylonian control. The stele, found at Susa in 1901, is now in the Louvre.

hechos/samsu-iluna-contra-los-casitas/re.texto: The ninth year of Samsu-iluna recalls the defeat of “the entire strength of the Kassite army”, the first known mention of that people in the sources.

hechos/rebelion-de-rim-sin-ii/titulo.texto: Revolt of Rim-Sin II against Samsu-iluna

hechos/rebelion-de-rim-sin-ii/resumen.texto: In year 9 of Samsu-iluna, a man who called himself Rim-Sin, perhaps a nephew of Rim-Sin I, rose up in Larsa; the revolt spread to some 26 cities, among them Uruk, Ur, Isin, Kisurra and Eshnunna. Samsu-iluna defeated it within a few years.

hechos/ejecucion-de-iluni-de-eshnunna/ti.texto: Samsu-iluna Captures and Executes Iluni of Eshnunna

hechos/ejecucion-de-iluni-de-eshnunna/re.texto: After a blow against the coalition, Samsu-iluna brought the king of Eshnunna, Iluni, to Babylon and had him executed by strangulation.

hechos/samsu-iluna-destruye-la-muralla-d.texto: Samsu-iluna Destroys the Wall of Isin

A year name from year 27 of Samsu-iluna says that he destroyed the wall of Isin. Soon afterward the irrigation systems of the Isin and Nippur region failed, and the southern cities were largely abandoned.

hechos/abandono-de-las-ciudades-del-sur/.texto: Abandonment of Southern Mesopotamian Cities under Samsu-iluna

The records of Ur, Uruk and Larsa end around year 10 of Samsu-iluna and those of Nippur and Isin around year 29; archaeology shows those cities almost empty. The cause is debated: war, failure of the canals, or change in the climate.

hechos/abandono-de-mashkan-shapir/resume.texto: The city, second capital of Larsa, was abandoned around 1720 BC, in the time of Samsu-iluna, as part of the general collapse of the sites in the region.

hechos/samsu-iluna-saquea-shubat-enlil/t.texto: Samsu-iluna Destroys Apum and Sacks Shubat-Enlil

hechos/samsu-iluna-saquea-shubat-enlil/r.texto: Samsu-iluna destroyed the city of Apum and killed its king Yakun-ashar around his year 24 (c. 1726 BC); Tell Leilan, the capital of Apum, was sacked. Another date places the incorporation of Apum into Babylon in 1728 BC, two years earlier, and the two cannot be reconciled. The following year he attacked Terqa.

hechos/dur-samsu-iluna/titulo.texto: Samsu-iluna Builds the Fortress of Dur-Samsu-iluna

hechos/dur-samsu-iluna/resumen.texto: Eshnunna rebelled in year 20 of Samsu-iluna and, in his year 24 (c. 1726 BC), the king built the fortress of Dur-Samsu-iluna to keep the region under control. An inscribed cylinder, found as a foundation deposit on Mound B at Khafajah, identifies the fort with that site.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-primera-dinastia-.texto: Ilum-ma-ili Founds the First Dynasty of the Sealand

A pretender named Ilum-ma-ili, who claimed to be a descendant of the last king of Isin, led a Sumerian revolt against Samsu-iluna and founded the dynasty of the Sealand, which dominated southern Sumer for almost three centuries. The date, c. 1725 BC, is very speculative.

hechos/saqueo-hitita-de-babilonia/resume.texto: Mursili I of the Hittites defeats Samsu-ditana, last king of the first dynasty of Babylon, and carries off the statue of Marduk from the Esagila; the city falls around 1595 BC in the middle chronology (1531 BC in the short one). The Amorite dynasty ends and the Kassites follow.

hechos/ascenso-de-los-casitas-en-babilon.texto: The Kassites Take Power in Babylon

After the Hittite sack, the Kassite dynasty ruled Babylon between 1595 and 1155 BC according to the middle chronology; the kings before Karaindash are hard to reconstruct because the lists contradict one another.

hechos/ulamburiash-conquista-el-pais-del.texto: Ulamburiash Defeats Ea-gamil and Reunifies Babylon
The Kassite king Ulamburiash defeated Ea-gamil, last king of the first dynasty of the Sealand, and reunified Babylon. The date is approximate.

hechos/karaindash-templo-de-uruk/titulo.texto: Karaindash Builds a Temple in Eanna

hechos/karaindash-templo-de-uruk/resumen.texto: Karaindash (15th century BC) had a small temple of original decoration built inside Eanna, the religious complex of Uruk. One of his inscriptions contains the first known mention of Karduniash, the Kassite name of Babylon.

hechos/fundacion-de-dur-kurigalzu/resume.texto: The Kassite king Kurigalzu I founds the city of Dur-Kurigalzu near present-day Baghdad at the beginning of the 14th century BC; it later became the Kassite capital. The city is mentioned in the toponym lists of the temple of the pharaoh Amenhotep III.

hechos/ashur-uballit-i-derrota-a-mitani/.texto: Ashur-uballit I defeats the Mitannian king Shuttarna III, which marks the full ascendancy of Assyria over the Hurro-Mitannians. He is the first king of the Middle Assyrian Empire.

hechos/matrimonio-de-burna-buriash-ii-y-.texto: Marriage of Burna-Buriash II to the Daughter of Ashur-uballit I
Burna-Buriash II of Babylon, who regarded Assyria as a vassal, ended up marrying Muballitat-Sherua, daughter of Ashur-uballit I; their son was Kara-hardash. The date is approximate.

hechos/matrimonio-de-una-hija-de-burna-b.texto: A Daughter of Burna-Buriash II Marries the Pharaoh Akhenaten
Burna-Buriash II married one of his daughters to the pharaoh Akhenaten, as part of the marriage alliances between the courts of the Late Bronze Age.

hechos/ashur-uballit-i-impone-a-kurigalz.texto: Ashur-uballit I Invades Babylon and Places Kurigalzu II

After an anti-Assyrian revolt against King Kara-hardash, grandson of Ashur-uballit I, in which he died, the army put Nazi-Bugash on the throne. The Assyrian king invaded Babylon, deposed him and placed Kurigalzu II. The latter later turned against Assyria, and Ashur-uballit I counterattacked and imposed a favorable treaty on him.

hechos/adad-nirari-i-somete-a-hanigalbat.texto: Adad-nirari I defeated the Mitannian king Shattuara, took him to Assur and forced him to swear vassalage; later, when his son Wasashatta rebelled, he sacked his cities. The date within the reign (c. 1305-1274 BC) is uncertain.

hechos/shalmaneser-i-derrota-a-shattuara.texto: Shalmaneser I Defeats Shattuara of Hanigalbat

In his second year, according to his Assur annals, Shalmaneser I defeated Shattuara, king of Hanigalbat, and his Hittite and Ahlamu allies, and turned the rest of the Mitannian kingdom into an Assyrian province. He is one of the first Assyrian kings to deport the defeated.

hechos/batalla-de-nihriya/resumen.texto: Battle between the Hittite king Tudhaliya IV and Assyria over the remains of Mitanni, in the upper Balikh. The texts that name it (KUB XXIII 99, KBo XVIII 24 and RS 34.165) give Shalmaneser I as the Assyrian king, and the year is uncertain; other scholars attribute it to his son Tukulti-Ninurta I, whose inscriptions boast of the deportation of 28 800 Hittite subjects.

hechos/fundacion-de-kar-tukulti-ninurta/.texto: When his relations with the priesthood of Assur deteriorated, Tukulti-Ninurta I built a new cult center of Ashur and perhaps a new capital north of Assur.

hechos/asesinato-de-tukulti-ninurta-i/re.texto: His sons rebelled, besieged him in Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta and killed him during the siege; one of them, Ashur-nadin-apli, succeeded him. The city was largely abandoned and the cult of Ashur returned to Assur.
