hechos/kidin-hutran-devasta-nippur/resum.texto: The Elamite king Kidin-Hutran, linked by marriage to the Kassite kings, devastated Nippur and complicated the position of the rulers that Assyria had set up in Babylon, who were deposed one after another until 1217 BC.

hechos/ninurta-apal-ekur-usurpa-el-trono.texto: Ninurta-apal-Ekur Usurps the Throne of Assyria

Ninurta-apal-Ekur took the throne of Assyria, styled himself king of the universe and priest of the god Ashur, and founded a line that reigned until Ashur-dan I. According to one source, the Babylonian king Marduk-apla-iddina I helped him come to power.

hechos/saqueo-elamita-de-babilonia/resum.texto: Shutruk-Nahhunte of Elam invaded Kassite Babylon around 1158 BC and carried off monuments from Babylon, Sippar and Eshnunna. Other dates give 1160 BC.

hechos/traslado-de-las-estelas-a-susa/ti.texto: The Stelae of Hammurabi and Naram-Sin Go to Susa

hechos/traslado-de-las-estelas-a-susa/re.texto: Among the monuments taken to Susa by Shutruk-Nahhunte was the victory stele of Naram-Sin of Akkad; the stele of the Code of Hammurabi was found at Susa in 1901 and, according to Scheil, the same king had taken it there.

hechos/fin-de-la-dinastia-casita/titulo.texto: Kutir-Nahhunte Defeats Enlil-nadin-ahi and Ends the Kassite Dynasty

hechos/fin-de-la-dinastia-casita/resumen.texto: According to later Babylonian texts, Kutir-Nahhunte, son of Shutruk-Nahhunte, defeated Enlil-nadin-ahi, the last Kassite king (c. 1157-1155 BC), and deported him to Susa with the Kassite nobles and the statue of Marduk, taken from the temples of Babylon. The king list records only the end of the dynasty.

hechos/redaccion-de-las-leyes-asirias-me.texto: The Middle Assyrian Laws Are Drafted
The three collections of Middle Assyrian laws were developed between 1450 and 1250 BC. The oldest copy discovered dates from the time of Tiglath-pileser I.

hechos/comercio-paleoasirio-con-kanesh/r.texto: Merchants of Assur settled in the karum of Kanesh, in Anatolia, and left more than 23 000 tablets documenting the trade. Around 1798-1740 BC level Ib recovered its prosperity under the control of Ishme-Dagan I.

hechos/puzur-ashur-i-funda-asiria/titulo.texto: Puzur-Ashur I Founds Assyria as an Independent City-State

hechos/puzur-ashur-i-funda-asiria/resume.texto: After the collapse of Ur III, Puzur-Ashur I is considered the founder of Assur as an independent state, c. 2025 BC. Some historians believe his dynasty began earlier, perhaps with Sulili.

hechos/nippur-casita-obras-mayores/resum.texto: The Kassites restored the Ekur of Nippur from Kurigalzu I onward; with Kadashman-Enlil, Kudur-Enlil and Shagarakti-Shuriash the major works were carried out. Thousands of texts come from their archives.

hechos/adad-nirari-i-palacio-en-kilizu/t.texto: Adad-nirari I Builds a Palace at Kilizu

hechos/adad-nirari-i-palacio-en-kilizu/r.texto: Four brick molds discovered in 2018 at Qasr Shemamok celebrate the construction of a palace by Adad-nirari I at Kilizu. The date within his reign is approximate.

hechos/hammurabi-vence-a-malgium/resumen.texto: The tenth year of Hammurabi commemorates a victory over Malgium, east of Babylon, with the support of Shamshi-Adad I and the king of Eshnunna. The city remained independent until c. 1761-1759 BC, when it suffered a fate similar to that of Mari.

hechos/guerra-elamita-contra-eshnunna-y-.texto: Elam Attacks Eshnunna and Faces a Coalition

With Siwe-palar-huppak as grand regent of Elam, the Elamites expanded over the Mesopotamian plain, attacked and subjugated Eshnunna with the initial support of Babylon and Mari, and then threatened the north of Babylon. A coalition of kingdoms from Mesopotamia and Syria repelled them with difficulty, thanks to troops from Mari and the north; Hammurabi and Rim-Sin I of Larsa allied against Elam, although the former contributed little.

hechos/silli-sin-rey-de-eshnunna/titulo.texto: Silli-Sin Accedes to the Throne of Eshnunna

hechos/silli-sin-rey-de-eshnunna/resumen.texto: After the withdrawal of the Elamite troops, Hammurabi considered annexing Eshnunna or putting a member of the local family on the throne; but the elites enthroned a section chief, Silli-Sin. A year of difficult negotiations with Babylon followed, and Silli-Sin married a daughter of Hammurabi.

hechos/hammurabi-derrota-a-la-coalicion-.texto: Hammurabi Defeats a Northern Coalition and Prevails in Assur

The name of Hammurabi's year 37 recalls his victory over a coalition of kings from Shubartum, Turukkum and Gutium, after which he deported people from the conquered lands and established his rule over Assur. The name of year 39 recalls another victory at Shubartum.

hechos/abi-eshuh-vence-a-los-casitas/res.texto: The fourth year name of Abi-eshuh recalls that he subdued the Kassite army.

hechos/abi-eshuh-contra-iluma-ilum/titul.texto: Abi-eshuh and the Tigris Dike against the Sealand

hechos/abi-eshuh-contra-iluma-ilum/lugar.texto: Lower course of the Tigris (site not specified)

hechos/abi-eshuh-contra-iluma-ilum/resum.texto: The Chronicle of the Ancient Kings recalls that Abi-eshuh dammed the Tigris in a failed attempt to capture Ilum-ma-ili, founder of the dynasty of the Sealand. It is a tradition from a chronicle preserved in late copies.

hechos/agum-kakrime-recupera-la-estatua-.texto: Agum-kakrime Restores the Statue of Marduk to the Esagila

According to the inscription of Agum-kakrime, the king recovered from Hana the statue of Marduk that the Hittites had carried off in the sack of Babylon and returned it to the renewed Esagila. The Prophecy of Marduk, a later text, gives 24 years between the abduction and the return; the inscription is known only from late Assyrian copies and there is no independent confirmation.

hechos/cartas-de-amarna-entre-kadashman-.texto: Letters between Kadashman-Enlil I and Amenhotep III

Letters EA 1 to EA 5 gather the correspondence of Kadashman-Enlil I of Babylon with the pharaoh Amenhotep III about marriages and gifts; only EA 1 and EA 5 were sent from Egypt to Babylon. They anchor the chronology of the period, because they fix a synchronism between the two reigns.

hechos/asiria-entra-en-la-diplomacia-de-.texto: Ashur-uballit I Writes to the Pharaoh

Ashur-uballit I sent the pharaoh letters (EA 15 and EA 16) that present Assyria as a power with the standing of an international interlocutor. In EA 15 he explains that his messenger goes to Egypt to see the country, and alludes to a period without contact between the two kingdoms. In EA 16 the pharaoh's name is broken, and most read it as Akhenaten.

hechos/batalla-de-sugagu/lugar.texto: Sugagu (on the Tigris, site not identified)

hechos/batalla-de-sugagu/resumen.texto: Two chronicles describe a clash between Kurigalzu II and the Assyrian king at Sugagu, on the Tigris, one day's march south of Assur. One gives the victory to Kurigalzu, although it confuses his opponent with Adad-nirari; the other gives it to Enlil-nirari and says that the districts were divided and the border fixed. The outcome may have been indecisive; a later kudurru of Kashtiliash IV recalls a donation by Kurigalzu to a servant for the war against Assyria.

hechos/batalla-de-kar-ishtar/resumen.texto: Nazi-Maruttash of Babylon fought the forces of Adad-nirari I at Kar-Ishtar of Ugarsallu. The Assyrians proclaimed a complete victory, with the plunder of the camp and the capture of the royal standards, and a gain of territory that pushed the frontier south; the Epic of Tukulti-Ninurta recalls it. Kadashman-Turgu, Nazi-Maruttash's successor, later accepted a treaty with Adad-nirari I.

hechos/salmanasar-i-funda-kalhu/titulo.texto: Shalmaneser I founds a settlement at Kalhu

hechos/salmanasar-i-funda-kalhu/resumen.texto: Kalhu began as a trading settlement founded under Shalmaneser I (c. 1274–1245 BC), on the route between Assur and Nineveh. It declined over time until Ashurnasirpal II chose it as capital in the 9th century BC.

hechos/zigurat-de-dur-kurigalzu/titulo.texto: The ziggurat of Dur-Kurigalzu is built

hechos/zigurat-de-dur-kurigalzu/resumen.texto: At the beginning of the 14th century BC, Kurigalzu I raised the ziggurat of the city he founded, dedicated to Enlil. Its remains at Aqar Quf rise about 52 m and for centuries were a landmark for caravans heading to Baghdad.

hechos/kidin-hutran-ataca-marad-e-isin/r.texto: In his second attack on Babylon, under King Adad-shuma-iddina, Kidin-Hutran of Elam struck Marad and Isin, according to the Chronicle P.

hechos/fundacion-de-dur-untash/resumen.texto: Untash-Napirisha built Dur-Untash (Chogha Zanbil), a cult complex to Inshushinak with a five-stage ziggurat and temples to other gods. The exact date depends on the chronology of his reign: the 14th or 13th century BC; the work continued after his death until its destruction by Ashurbanipal.

hechos/tablilla-im-67118-de-geometria/ti.texto: Tablet IM 67118 solves a geometry problem

hechos/tablilla-im-67118-de-geometria/re.texto: An Old Babylonian tablet from the kingdom of Eshnunna, found at Tell al-Dhiba'i, gives the solution to a problem about a rectangle with a given area and diagonal and checks it with the Pythagorean theorem. It is dated to around the reign of Ibal-pi-El II.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-segunda-dinastia-.texto: Marduk-kabit-ahheshu founds the Second Dynasty of Isin

After the Elamite fall of the Kassite dynasty, Marduk-kabit-ahheshu (c. 1153–1136 BC) founded the Second Dynasty of Isin, which ruled Babylon until c. 1022 BC. The Babylonian King List C gives him an 18-year reign.

hechos/revuelta-contra-kara-hardash/titu.texto: Anti-Assyrian revolt against Kara-hardash and usurpation of Nazi-Bugash

hechos/revuelta-contra-kara-hardash/resu.texto: Kara-hardash, king of Babylon and grandson of the Assyrian king Ashur-uballit I, was murdered in an anti-Assyrian revolt. The army put Nazi-Bugash (or Shuzigash), a Kassite, on the throne, until Ashur-uballit I intervened and deposed him.

hechos/naram-sin-de-eshnunna-ataca-ekall.texto: Naram-Sin of Eshnunna attacks Ekallatum, and Shamshi-Adad I goes into exile in Babylon
Naram-Sin of Eshnunna attacked Ekallatum around 1823 BC, and Shamshi-Adad I, son of Ila-kabkabu, fled to Babylon. He returned on the death of Naram-Sin, around 1809 BC.

hechos/samsu-iluna-reconstruye-seis-fort.texto: Samsu-iluna rebuilds six fortresses near Nippur
In the 18th year of his reign (c. 1732 BC), Samsu-iluna had six fortresses rebuilt around Nippur, perhaps to keep the city under Babylonian control.

hechos/samsu-iluna-contra-ilum-ma-ili/re.texto: Ilum-ma-ili, who claimed to be a descendant of the last king of Isin, led a Sumerian revolt. Samsu-iluna marched against him in a battle with no clear result; in a second battle, some time later, Ilum-ma-ili won and founded the First Dynasty of the Sea Land.

hechos/kish-bajo-control-babilonio/resum.texto: In the time of Sin-muballit of Babylon (c. 1813–1792 BC), Kish was firmly under Babylonian control. Hammurabi and Samsu-iluna carried out major works there, including the rebuilding of the wall.

lugares/mashkan-shapir/resumen.texto: City of the god Nergal, walled by Sin-iddinam of Larsa, and second capital of Larsa under Rim-Sin I. It was abandoned around 1720 BC, in the reign of Samsu-iluna.

lugares/shaduppum/resumen.texto: Administrative center of the kingdom of Eshnunna, near present-day Baghdad. The Old Babylonian levels yielded the tablets of the Laws of Eshnunna.

lugares/tell-al-rimah/resumen.texto: Site west of Mosul proposed as Karana, Qattara or Razama; its Old Babylonian archive includes that of Abu-tab. It was reoccupied in the Late Bronze Age under Mitanni.

lugares/assur/resumen.texto: City-state on the Tigris and center of the god Ashur, capital of Old and Middle Assyria. It was occupied for about 3000 years, until it was sacked by the Sasanians around the 3rd century AD.

lugares/dur-kurigalzu/resumen.texto: City founded by the Kassite king Kurigalzu I at the beginning of the 14th century BC, near present-day Baghdad (Aqar Quf), with a ziggurat and temples. It was abandoned after the fall of the Kassite dynasty.

lugares/kar-tukulti-ninurta/resumen.texto: New city and cult center of Ashur, founded by Tukulti-Ninurta I north of Assur. It was largely abandoned after the king's death.

lugares/kanesh/resumen.texto: Trading center on the Anatolian plateau where the karum of the Assyrian merchants was established; its lower town yielded more than 23,000 cuneiform tablets.

lugares/malgium/resumen.texto: Mesopotamian city tentatively identified with Tell Yassir. It survived to the end of the second millennium and is named in two kudurrus of Meli-Shipak.

lugares/me-turan/resumen.texto: City of the Diyala founded at the beginning of the second millennium, controlled by Eshnunna, where a fragment of the Laws of Eshnunna was found.

lugares/tell-ishchali/resumen.texto: Site in the Diyala identified with Nerebtum, with the temple of Kititum. Occupied until c. 1762 BC, when Babylon destroyed it.

lugares/tell-sifr/resumen.texto: Site east of Larsa identified with Kutalla, occupied in the Isin-Larsa and Old Babylonian periods.

lugares/tell-khaiber/resumen.texto: Fortified site in the southern Mesopotamian marshes, about 20 km from Ur, occupied mainly in the time of the First Dynasty of the Sealand; an archive of 152 tablets dates it to the reign of Ayadaragalama. It is a site of that kingdom, whose capital is unknown. Occupied from c. 1500 BC.

lugares/esagila/resumen.texto: Temple of Marduk in Babylon, south of the ziggurat Etemenanki, where the main statue of the god was kept. His statue of Marduk was surrounded by images of the cities subjected to Babylon since the 18th century BC.

lugares/dur-katlimmu/resumen.texto: City of the lower Khabur, part of Mitanni and Hanigalbat, and later provincial capital of Middle Assyria.

lugares/tell-shemshara/resumen.texto: Site on the Lesser Zab with a Middle Bronze Age tablet archive linked to Shamshi-Adad I.

lugares/sippar-amnanum/resumen.texto: City about 70 km north of Babylon, occupied since the Akkadian Empire and developed mainly in the Old Babylonian period.

lugares/kilizu/resumen.texto: Site south of Erbil with Hurrian, Middle Assyrian and Neo-Assyrian remains, called Kilizu in the Assyrian period. In 2018 brick molds were found that mention a palace built by Adad-nirari I. There was light occupation from the Hassuna period, and later in the Halaf, Uruk, Nineveh V, Early Dynastic and Old Babylonian periods.

lugares/palacio-de-mari/resumen.texto: Residence of the kings of Mari, rebuilt at the beginning of the shakkanakku period, in the 22nd century BC. Zimri-Lim lived in it without changing its plan, with a throne room, the Palm Court and a women's quarter; the royal archive tablets were found there. The armies of Hammurabi occupied it in 1761 BC and destroyed it systematically in 1759 BC.

lugares/tell-muhammad/resumen.texto: Site in the Diyala valley, on the outskirts of Baghdad, near Tell Harmal. Its ancient name is unknown; Diniktum, Banaia and even Akkad have been proposed. An early Old Babylonian level (19th century BC) and later ones yielded about 70 contract tablets from a family of merchants, and in 1850 J. F. Jones found bronze maces with an inscription of Hammurabi.

lugares/kalhu/resumen.texto: Assyrian city on the Tigris south of Mosul that originated as a trading settlement founded under Shalmaneser I (c. 1274–1245 BC). It declined until Ashurnasirpal II chose it as capital in the 9th century BC.

lugares/chogha-zanbil/resumen.texto: Elamite complex about 30 km southeast of Susa, founded by Untash-Napirisha, mainly in honor of Inshushinak, with a five-stage ziggurat in a sacred enclosure of three concentric walls. The construction date is uncertain because of the chronology of that reign (14th or 13th century BC); the site remained occupied until Ashurbanipal destroyed it around 645 BC.

lugares/haft-tepe/resumen.texto: Site about 15 km southwest of Susa where possible remains of the Elamite city of Kabnak were found, the political center in the reign of Tepti-Ahar, last king of the Kidinuid dynasty in the 15th century BC. It has a large funerary complex with vaulted tombs and a stela, written in the Babylonian of the period, with funerary rites and duties.

lugares/tell-sabi-abyad/resumen.texto: Site in the Balikh valley, in northern Syria. In the Middle Assyrian period it had a fortress (c. 1550–1250 BC according to its dating) and more than 400 tablets from the late 13th and the 12th century BC; after a fire shortly after 1180 BC, Assyrian administrators stayed there until the end of the 12th century BC.

lugares/tell-fekheriye/resumen.texto: Site in the Khabur basin, securely identified with Sikkan, attested from c. 2000 BC. It was proposed as Washukanni, the capital of Mitanni, a hypothesis not confirmed that some specialists reject and others, such as Stefano de Martino, support on the basis of recent German excavations.

lugares/failaka/resumen.texto: Kuwaiti island inhabited from c. 2000 BC by merchants from Ur. It was part of Dilmun, where it was called Agarum, “land of Inzak”; a seal found there, from around 1650 BC, preserves the name of a king of Dilmun, Sumu-lel, with the title “servant of Inzak of Agarum.”

lugares/tell-al-dhibai/resumen.texto: Site of the kingdom of Eshnunna on the outskirts of Baghdad, 3 km northeast of Shaduppum (Tell Harmal). Zaralulu has been proposed as its ancient name, and it was occupied mainly in the Isin-Larsa and Old Babylonian periods; tablet IM 67118 was excavated there in 1962.

lugares/arrapha/resumen.texto: City or kingdom in the northeast of present-day Iraq, thought to have been located at Kirkuk. It is recorded in writing from the Ur III period; it was a trading center in the 18th century BC and, in the 15th and 14th centuries BC, the capital of a small Hurrian kingdom vassal to Mitanni. With Middle Assyria it was fully incorporated into Assyria. Its first written record is from the Neo-Sumerian period, 22nd-21st centuries BC.

lugares/tell-al-fakhar/resumen.texto: Tell 45 km southwest of Kirkuk with a phase from the middle of the second millennium BC (Mitanni and Kassite period): a large building of at least 17 rooms, called the Green Palace, where an archive of about 800 tablets was found. It has been proposed as the ancient Kurruhanni, an identification that is debated.

lugares/tell-taban/resumen.texto: Site on the Khabur, the ancient Tabatum, a regional center in the Mari tablets of the 18th century BC. Between the mid-14th and early 12th centuries BC a local dynasty, vassal to the Middle Assyrian kings, governed Tabetu and styled itself «king of Tabetu and the land of Mari»; the excavations yielded Old Babylonian and Middle Assyrian tablets. It appears in the Mari tablets of the 18th century BC as Ṭābatum; a local dynasty governed it between the mid-14th and early 12th centuries BC.

lugares/shibaniba/resumen.texto: Site 20 km northeast of Mosul, called Shibaniba in the Middle Assyrian period. It shows traces of occupation from the Uruk period and of Hurrian presence in the middle of the second millennium BC, and yielded 91 Middle Assyrian tablets dated c. 1400–1000 BC.

lugares/tell-bazmusian/resumen.texto: Tell on the Lesser Zab, now under the waters of Lake Dukan, with 16 occupation levels. Level III, from the late second millennium BC, had a single-room temple and fragments of tablets in the Middle Assyrian style.

lugares/tell-barri/resumen.texto: Tell on the Khabur, the ancient Kahat, attested in the 18th-century BC Mari archives. It was a religious center under Mitanni, and under Adad-nirari I of Assyria a large palace was built there.
